_note: The enshittification ledger. Dated, sourced incidents only. vendor_risk 0-3 is computed from this, never from reputation. A vendor with a documented incident cannot be scored 0 no matter how good the current product is.

_scale.0: No documented incident of a shipped device losing function after purchase.
_scale.1: One disputed or narrow incident, or a pattern alleged but not established.
_scale.2: At least one established incident of shipped devices losing function.
_scale.3: Repeated, established, cross-jurisdiction pattern of removing function from devices already sold.
_scale._note_on_misrepresentation: Loss of function is the primary axis, but it is not the only one that matters to this catalog. A vendor caught misrepresenting whether its device operates locally has attacked the exact claim this site exists to check, and scores here on the same scale — a device that was never doing what the box said is not meaningfully different, to a reader, from one that stopped.
_scale._note_on_forced_security_patches: Motive is not the test; loss of function is. A forced update that removes NO function is not an incident and does not belong here — it is firmware_ota_forced on the device record, which already tells a reader the vendor can change their device without consent. A forced update that DOES remove function is an incident, scored on the normal scale, with the security motive recorded in the description rather than discounted from the score. Adopted 2026-09-14 over QNAP; applies to every vendor. The consequence is deliberate: a vendor can sit at 0 here and still be one you would keep off the internet, because 0 means "no documented removal of function", not "safe".

anova.name: Anova Culinary
anova.summary: Announced it would end app and cloud support for first-generation Precision Cookers, then cancelled the plan before it took effect. Separately introduced an app subscription that binds new accounts only. Scored 1 because the threat to already-sold hardware was withdrawn — the ledger scores what happened, not what was announced.

incidents.description: Anova introduced a $2/month or $10/year subscription for app remote control and monitoring, announced 2024-08-14 and effective 2024-08-21 for accounts created from that date onward; pre-existing accounts were grandfathered free. Announced at the same time: a plan to end app and cloud support entirely for original first-generation Precision Cookers from September 2025. The subscription binds only new buyers and does not gate the cook itself, which runs from the device's own touchscreen — so it does not on its own justify a higher score.

Anova cancelled the end-of-support plan before it took effect, in its own words committing 'to keeping all our cookers fully supported', noting original units are now over ten years old and still running on maintained legacy infrastructure. This is why the entry is 1 and not 2: shipped hardware was threatened and then was not harmed.

anova.verdict: The cooker itself is unaffected by any of this — time and temperature are set on its own touchscreen and the cook runs with no phone, account or subscription, which is why anova-precision-cooker-3 is D2. What the ledger records is that Anova has twice repriced the software around already-sold hardware and once proposed withdrawing it. Buy it for the cooker, not for the app.

bambu-lab.name: Bambu Lab
bambu-lab.summary: Shipped firmware that put previously-free local printing behind cloud authentication, then documented a way back to full local control. Scored 1 rather than 2 because the loss was remediable without hardware changes — but it did ship, and anyone who took the update without knowing about Developer Mode lost local function until they found it.

incidents.description: Firmware 01.08.03.00 (X1 series, 2025-01-17) introduced a mandatory 'Authorization Control System' requiring Bambu Connect cloud authentication to bind the printer, start a print job — over LAN as well as cloud — access remote video, or update firmware. Previously-free local and third-party paths, including OrcaSlicer integration, stopped working for anyone who applied it. Two things keep this at 1 rather than 2: the update could be declined outright, and Bambu documented a Developer Mode plus LAN Only path restoring full local MQTT/FTP with no cloud account, since extended to the A-series that bambu-lab-a1 belongs to. Note the mitigation arrived alongside the backlash rather than ahead of it, so a reader who wants to score this harder has grounds.
Independent coverage of the rollout and the resulting backlash from the OrcaSlicer and third-party-accessory community, including Bambu's public acknowledgement of the reaction.

bambu-lab.verdict: Turn on Developer Mode and LAN Only before you need them, and decline firmware you have not read the notes for. The local path is real, documented and currently maintained — which is why bambu-lab-a1 is D2 — but January 2025 established that it is a setting Bambu controls rather than a property of the printer.

brother.name: Brother Industries
brother.summary: Accused in 2025 of degrading third-party toner behaviour via firmware and of pulling older firmware from support portals. Brother denies it. The allegation is credible enough to record and not established enough to score higher.

incidents.description: Right-to-repair advocates alleged firmware updates degraded third-party toner function, including colour registration on colour models. Brother denies its updates block third-party consumables and attributes the reports to variation in third-party toner quality. Not independently established either way.
Brother's public denial, reported alongside the user complaints.

brother.verdict: Prefer Brother models with no network interface, where the dispute is structurally moot — the printer cannot fetch an update on its own. On networked Brother models, decline firmware updates unless you need a specific fix.

chamberlain.name: Chamberlain Group (myQ, LiftMaster)
chamberlain.summary: Systematically closed a previously open ecosystem on hardware already installed in customers' garages: dropped HomeKit, then Google Assistant, then shut off third-party API access entirely.

incidents.description: Discontinued the official Apple HomeKit integration for myQ.
Ended support for Google Assistant.

Blocked all third-party API access to myQ, breaking working integrations on devices customers already owned. Home Assistant removed its myQ integration in the 2023.12 release. Chamberlain's stated reason was preventing 'unauthorized usage' of its ecosystem.

chamberlain.verdict: Assume any myQ feature that depends on Chamberlain's servers can be withdrawn without notice, because it has been, three times. The openers themselves remain fine offline. If you want local control, plan on ratgdo from the start rather than hoping the app stays useful.

eufy.name: eufy (Anker Innovations)
eufy.summary: Marketed cameras as local-storage-only, then was shown to upload identifiable thumbnail images to its cloud with cloud storage disabled, and to serve camera streams that could be opened in VLC without encryption or authentication. Anker denied, then admitted, then re-architected.

incidents.description: Security researcher Paul Moore showed a eufy Doorbell Dual uploading face thumbnails and user information to eufy's cloud while the device was configured for local storage only. Anker initially denied the behaviour, then conceded images were uploaded 'for notification purposes'.

Camera streams were shown to be retrievable in VLC with no encryption and no authentication, contradicting eufy's marketing. Anker admitted the streams were not encrypted as claimed and committed to moving all cameras to WebRTC with AES/RSA encryption.
Class action filed alleging eufy security cameras secretly uploaded user images and live footage to the cloud contrary to its local-storage marketing.

eufy.verdict: Treat any eufy local-storage claim as unverified until confirmed by packet capture rather than by the vendor's own description. The hardware may be fine; the vendor's account of it has been wrong before on precisely this point.

hp.name: HP Inc.
hp.summary: Repeatedly shipped firmware that disabled third-party cartridges on printers customers already owned, across multiple jurisdictions and more than a decade. Settled repeatedly without admitting wrongdoing.

incidents.description: A firmware update enabled Dynamic Security on some already-sold printer models, blocking non-HP cartridges. Customers were not notified the update would impede function and had no way to opt out.

Class action settled with court approval. No customer payout and no admission of wrongdoing; owners of 21 named models gained the option to decline Dynamic Security firmware, and to downgrade firmware on those models only.
Earlier Dynamic Security settlements: $1.5M in California (2018), AUD$50 per affected customer in Australia (2018), EUR10M in Italy (2020), $1.35M in Europe (2022).

hp.verdict: Assume any networked HP printer may lose third-party cartridge support via an update you cannot decline. Only models explicitly covered by the 2025 settlement have a documented opt-out.

qnap.name: QNAP Systems
qnap.summary: Force-installed firmware on NAS units whose owners had switched automatic updates off, and that update cost some of them working function. The motive was a live ransomware campaign, which is recorded here rather than discounted — but the reader's takeaway is different in kind from HP or Sonos: this is not a vendor monetising hardware you bought, it is a vendor that will reach into it without asking.

incidents.description: During the DeadBolt ransomware campaign, which had encrypted roughly 3,600 internet-exposed units, QNAP force-installed firmware 5.0.0.1891 on customer NAS devices — including, per owner and admin reports, on devices where automatic updates had been explicitly disabled. QNAP confirmed to BleepingComputer that it forced the install, citing a remote-code-execution flaw fixed in that build. Two losses followed for some owners: iSCSI connections stopped working after the update, and users who had bought a decryption key and were mid-recovery found the update had removed the ransomware executable and ransom screen, leaving them unable to finish decrypting their own data. The security motive is real and is why this is scored 2 rather than higher; the loss of function is why it is scored at all.

QNAP's own DeadBolt security advisory (QSA-22-02), confirming the campaign, the affected QTS versions and the company's instruction to update immediately and to disable internet-facing access — the vendor-side record of the event above.

qnap.verdict: Buy it, then keep it off the open internet — which is what you should do with any NAS, and what QNAP's own advisory tells you to do. The hardware is not the risk and nothing here is subscription-driven: a QNAP NAS still administers entirely from its local web interface with no account. What the ledger records is that the update channel is not yours to control, so assume any QNAP firmware can arrive unasked. That is a reason to firewall it, not a reason to avoid it.

ring.name: Ring (Amazon)
ring.summary: Moved features that shipped free onto already-sold doorbells and cameras behind the paid Ring Protect plan, and raised the plan price sharply in the same period.

incidents.description: From 29 March 2024, Home and Away modes — and the Live View customisation tied to them — required a Ring Protect subscription on video doorbells and cameras, for existing owners as well as new buyers. Ring Alarm owners who bought before that date were grandfathered; doorbell and camera owners were not.
The entry Ring plan rose to $4.99/month or $49.99/year, reported as a 43% increase over the pre-March-2024 price.

ring.verdict: Assume any Ring feature that is free today may require a subscription later, on hardware you already own. The March 2024 change did not grandfather camera and doorbell owners.

sonos.name: Sonos
sonos.summary: Twice removed function from speakers already in customers' homes, five years apart, and in between split its own installed base into supported and legacy halves. Scored alongside Chamberlain rather than Ring because this is a repeated pattern across separate mechanisms — a deliberate bricking feature, an end-of-support split, and a software rewrite — not one recurring commercial decision.

incidents.description: The Trade Up programme's 'Recycle Mode' permanently deactivated working speakers in exchange for 30% off a new one: confirming it in the app started a 21-day countdown after which the unit was bricked with no way to recover it, and recyclers could not resell or reuse the hardware. Eligible units included the Connect, Connect:Amp, ZP80/90/100/120 and Play:5 (Gen 1). Opt-in rather than forced — which is the honest qualification — but it destroyed functioning hardware by design. Withdrawn in March 2020 after sustained criticism; the discount now validates a serial number instead, and units already set to recycle could not be reversed.

Announced that a set of 'legacy' products would stop receiving software updates and new features from May 2020. The units kept playing, so this is the weakest of the three on the loss-of-function axis — but it partitioned existing systems, because a legacy device sharing a household system constrained what the rest of that system could do.

The 7 May app rewrite shipped without features that worked on already-sold speakers the day before: alarms and sleep timers, local music library search and management, playlist editing, SonosNet Wi-Fi settings, and much of the accessibility support blind users relied on. The old app could not be kept. The CEO apologised, put the fixes on a public Trello board, and estimated $20-30M to repair; annual revenue fell 4% and he left the company in January 2025.

sonos.verdict: The speakers are well made and the hardware is not the problem — the control layer is, and Sonos owns it entirely. There is no local-only mode: setup requires a Sonos account, so every unit is bound to a company that has twice decided what your existing hardware would stop doing. Buy it for what it does today, not for what it will still do in ten years, and prefer a bar that speaks HDMI-ARC or optical if longevity matters more than multi-room.

viofo.name: VIOFO
viofo.summary: No incident found. Operates no cloud service for its dashcams at all, sells radio-free and radio-equipped models side by side, and distributes firmware as SD-card files rather than over the air.
viofo.verdict: Structurally low risk: with no cloud and no OTA channel, there is no mechanism by which a shipped VIOFO camera could be changed after purchase.

withings.name: Withings
withings.summary: Community reports of features disappearing from already-owned devices and of in-app lockouts pending acceptance of new terms. Not corroborated by independent reporting at the time of writing; scored as alleged-but-not-established.

incidents.description: An r/withings open letter (357 upvotes, 150+ comments) collects owner reports of a BPM Connect losing sync capability and a ScanWatch losing SpO2/heart features, and of users locked out of already-purchased devices until new in-app data-sharing terms were accepted. A targeted search for independent reporting of a specific, dated removal found none — coverage in the same period describes features being ADDED by firmware update. The allegation is consistent and multi-user but rests on one community source.

withings.verdict: Watch, do not yet condemn. If a dated, independently-reported removal surfaces, this becomes a 2. Recheck on the next refresh pass.
